newsitem.title: JAPAN: Boom in samurai bonds sparks risk control concerns.
newsitem.headline: Boom in samurai bonds sparks risk control concerns.

text.p: A slew of samurai bond issues by borrowers with low credit ratings are making Japanese authorities think they may need some way of resolving problems in the event of a default, market sources said on Wednesday.

Japan's Ministry of Finance abolished samurai bond eligibility standards in January, opening the door for foreign issuers which have low credit ratings but want to issue such bonds, and this has spurred the recent issuing boom.
"Personally, I feel that there is a need to come up with some kind of measurement to cope, particularly in times of actual default," an official at the ministry said.
"I see it as a problem, that we do not have any resolution scheme for when trouble actually occurs," he said.
Samurais are yen-denominated bonds issued in Japan by a non-Japanese borrower.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) issued a report last Wednesday warning emerging-market borrowers and retail investors in Germany and Japan of the risks posed by the mushrooming issuance of yen- and mark-denominated bonds.
The IMF said the sharp increase in such issues has been led by countries in Latin America, although some eastern European nations have also been active borrowers.
"Basically, we feel the same way as what the IMF mentioned in that report," the MOF official said.

The ministry official said concerns about repayment problems have burgeoned particularly after Bulgaria's Mineralbank failed to redeem five billion yen worth of samurai bonds to Japanese creditors when they matured in June.
MOF avoided direct comment on the Mineralbank problem because its bonds were privately placed, but it has been monitoring the situation carefully.

Underwriting sources estimate the volume of samurai bond issues from January up to now total a record high of about 2.9 trillion yen. Of that, about 20 percent are of sub-investment grade, which means a credit rating of below triple B (BBB).
They said borrowers' eagerness to issue bonds waned a bit particularly after the Bulgarian problem, but their appetite has grown again.

Mexico and the National Bank of Romania, both of which are of sub-investment grade, have recently launched samurai bonds, following a major wave of issues by Brazil and Turkey shortly after MOF's deregulation.

"Depending on the syndicators, Mexican bonds have mixed sales status. But in general, they are well-received by investors," one syndicate source said. "Romanian bonds have been actively absorbed due to their high coupon."
Underwriting sources said more sovereign issues with low credit ratings are likely to be launched by Argentina, Turkey, Poland and Hungary in the foreseeable future.
"From our point of view, we don't want new regulations," said Masaru Hamazaki, deputy manager at Yamaichi Research Institute.

"But more important, securities firms need to acquire knowledge with which to inform the investors," he said. "It's our role to analyse in depth to provide investors with full information about issuers."
Another MOF official said there was no need to create new rules, adding: "The ministry had deregulated the eligibility rules only recently... It's unlikely the government will set up rules again."
"We believe investors will make decisions on their own good judgement. It is not our duty to interfere with that," he said.
